core: The two clauses of the Fourth Amendment and the fact that the operative command is reasonableness, not a universal warrant requirement
The threshold question of what counts as a 'search': Katz v. United States and Justice Harlan's two-part reasonable-expectation-of-privacy formulation
The revival of the property/trespass theory in United States v. Jones, added to rather than substituted for Katz
Technology cases that apply the threshold test: Kyllo v. United States (sense-enhancing technology aimed at the home) and Carpenter v. United States (historical cell-site location information)

What counts as a seizure of a person: the Mendenhall 'free to leave' formulation, Florida v. Bostick's 'free to decline or terminate the encounter' restatement, California v. Hodari D.'s submission requirement, and Torres v. Madrid on physical force
The elements a warrant must have: probable cause under the Illinois v. Gates totality-of-the-circumstances standard, oath or affirmation, particularity, and a neutral judicial officer
The mechanics of a federal search warrant under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41

The major recognized exceptions to the warrant requirement: consent (Schneckloth v. Bustamonte), exigent circumstances (Kentucky v. King), search incident to lawful arrest (Chimel v. California, Arizona v. Gant, Riley v. California), the automobile exception (Carroll v. United States), plain view (Horton v. California), and the Terry stop and frisk
The exclusionary rule as the principal remedy (Mapp v. Ohio) and the good-faith exception (United States v. Leon), stated briefly with a pointer to the constitutional-protections lesson
The rule that state constitutions may impose greater restrictions on police than the federal floor (Oregon v. Hass)
Florida v. Jardines as the curtilage application of the trespass route to 'search'
Limits on third-party consent under Georgia v. Randolph, and the refusal to make exigency categorical in Missouri v. McNeely and Lange v. California
California v. Acevedo extending the automobile exception to containers inside a vehicle

Searches whose purpose is not ordinary criminal investigation: administrative inspections (Camara), vehicle inventories (South Dakota v. Opperman), and special needs (Skinner v. Railway Labor Executives' Assn.)
Fourth Amendment standing after Rakas v. Illinois, and the handoff from the right to the remedy
supporting: Payton v. New York's 'firm line at the entrance to the house' and the arrest-warrant/search-warrant distinction
That the Fourth Amendment restrains government actors, and reaches state and local officers through the Fourteenth Amendment
The distinction between probable cause and the lesser quantum of suspicion Terry requires
Riley's practical point that a warrant application is faster than it used to be, and that exigency remains available
outOfScope: The Fifth, Sixth, Eighth and Fourteenth Amendment framework and the full history of the exclusionary rule, its exceptions, and the deterrence debate (covered by the published constitutional-protections lesson)
The objective-reasonableness standard for police use of force under Graham v. Connor and Tennessee v. Garner (covered by the published use-of-force lesson)
Discretionary decision-making by officers as an organizational and behavioral matter (covered by the published police-discretion lesson)
Community policing philosophy and practice (assigned to another worker)
Court hierarchy and jurisdiction (assigned to another worker)
The procedural sequence from arrest through trial, including charging, bail, and suppression hearings as procedural stages (assigned to another worker)
Any instruction about how a person might avoid detection or defeat a lawful search
Border and checkpoint searches, school and probation searches, drug-testing regimes beyond the Skinner example, federal wiretap statutes, and civil remedies under 42 U.S.C. 1983 and Bivens

claims.claim: The Fourth Amendment contains two clauses: a reasonableness clause securing persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures, and a warrant clause requiring probable cause, oath or affirmation, and particular description of the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.

In Katz v. United States (1967) the Court held that attaching an electronic listening device to the outside of a public telephone booth was a search, that the Fourth Amendment protects people rather than places, and that the reach of the Amendment cannot turn on physical intrusion; Justice Harlan's concurrence stated the twofold requirement that a person exhibit an actual (subjective) expectation of privacy and that the expectation be one society is prepared to recognize as reasonable.
The Court also said in Katz that what a person knowingly exposes to the public, even in his own home or office, is not a subject of Fourth Amendment protection.

In United States v. Jones (2012) the Court held that the Government's attachment of a GPS device to a vehicle and its use to monitor the vehicle's movements is a search, reasoning that a physical intrusion on a constitutionally enumerated 'effect' for the purpose of obtaining information is a search, and stating that the Katz reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test has been added to, but not substituted for, the common-law trespassory test.

In Kyllo v. United States (2001) the Court held that where the Government uses a device not in general public use to explore details of a private home that would previously have been unknowable without physical intrusion, the surveillance is a search and is presumptively unreasonable without a warrant.

In Carpenter v. United States (2018) the Court held that the Government's acquisition of historical cell-site location information was a Fourth Amendment search, that a Stored Communications Act order under 18 U.S.C. 2703(d) resting on 'reasonable grounds' falls short of probable cause, and that the decision is narrow and leaves case-specific exceptions such as exigent circumstances available.

The 'free to leave' formulation for when a person has been seized appears in Justice Stewart's opinion in United States v. Mendenhall (1980), which was joined as to that part only by Justice Rehnquist; the Court there also listed circumstances indicating a seizure, including the threatening presence of several officers, display of a weapon, physical touching, or language or tone indicating that compliance might be compelled.

In Florida v. Bostick (1991) the Court rejected a per se rule that every police encounter on a bus is a seizure and held the appropriate test is whether, taking into account all the circumstances, a reasonable passenger would feel free to decline the officers' requests or otherwise terminate the encounter.

In California v. Hodari D. (1991) the Court held that a seizure of the person requires either the application of physical force, however slight, or, absent that, submission to an officer's show of authority; a suspect who keeps running after an officer's show of authority is not yet seized.

In Torres v. Madrid (2021) the Court held that the application of physical force to the body of a person with intent to restrain is a seizure even if the person does not submit and is not subdued, and that the inquiry is whether the challenged conduct objectively manifests an intent to restrain.

In Illinois v. Gates (1983) the Court abandoned the rigid Aguilar-Spinelli two-pronged test and adopted a totality-of-the-circumstances approach, describing the issuing magistrate's task as a practical, common-sense decision whether there is a fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place, with a reviewing court asking only whether the magistrate had a substantial basis for that conclusion.

Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41 requires a judge to issue a search warrant only on probable cause, requires the warrant to identify the person or property to be searched and any person or property to be seized, commands execution within a specified time no longer than 14 days and during the daytime unless the judge for good cause authorizes otherwise, requires an inventory and a receipt, requires the warrant to be returned to the designated judge, and provides that a defendant may move to suppress evidence in the trial court as Rule 12 provides.

In Payton v. New York (1980) the Court held that the Fourth Amendment prohibits police from making a warrantless and nonconsensual entry into a suspect's home to make a routine felony arrest, describing the Amendment as drawing a firm line at the entrance to the house that may not be crossed absent exigent circumstances.

In Schneckloth v. Bustamonte (1973) the Court held that when the subject of a search is not in custody and the government justifies the search by consent, it must show the consent was voluntary judged by the totality of the circumstances, and that knowledge of the right to refuse is a factor to be considered but need not be proved.

In Kentucky v. King (2011) the Court held that the exigent circumstances rule applies when the police do not create the exigency by engaging or threatening to engage in conduct that violates the Fourth Amendment, and identified the need to prevent the imminent destruction of evidence as one recognized exigency.

In Chimel v. California (1969) the Court limited a search incident to arrest to the arrestee's person and the area within his immediate control, meaning the area from which he might gain possession of a weapon or destructible evidence, and held that searching other rooms or closed areas requires a warrant absent a recognized exception.

In Arizona v. Gant (2009) the Court held that police may search the passenger compartment of a vehicle incident to a recent occupant's arrest only if it is reasonable to believe the arrestee might access the vehicle at the time of the search or that the vehicle contains evidence of the offense of arrest.

In Riley v. California (2014) the Court held that police generally may not, without a warrant, search digital information on a cell phone seized from a person who has been arrested, reasoning that digital data cannot be used as a weapon and that the Chimel rationales do not extend to it, while noting that exigent circumstances may still justify a warrantless search in particular cases.

In Carroll v. United States (1925) the Court held that the search of a movable vehicle for contraband does not depend on a right to arrest the driver and is lawful if the officer stopping and searching the vehicle has probable cause to believe it contains contraband, grounding the distinction in early congressional statutes that treated goods in transit differently from goods concealed in a dwelling.

In Horton v. California (1990) the Court held that inadvertence is not a necessary condition of a plain-view seizure, and restated the conditions that are required: the officer must not have violated the Fourth Amendment in arriving at the place from which the object could be plainly viewed, the object's incriminating character must be immediately apparent, and the officer must have a lawful right of access to the object itself.

In Terry v. Ohio (1968) the Court held that a police officer restraining a person's freedom to walk away has seized that person and that a careful exploration of the outer surfaces of clothing for weapons is a search, and required the officer to point to specific and articulable facts which, taken together with rational inferences from those facts, reasonably warrant the intrusion rather than an inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or hunch.

Mapp v. Ohio (1961) made the exclusionary rule binding on the states, and United States v. Leon (1984) created a good-faith exception for evidence obtained by officers acting in objectively reasonable reliance on a warrant issued by a detached and neutral magistrate but later found invalid.

The Supreme Court has stated that a State is free as a matter of its own law to impose greater restrictions on police activity than federal constitutional standards require, though it may not impose such restrictions as a matter of federal constitutional law.

In Florida v. Jardines (2013) the Court held that using a trained drug-detection dog on the front porch of a home to investigate its contents is a search within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment, because the front porch is curtilage and therefore part of the home for Fourth Amendment purposes.

In Georgia v. Randolph (2006) the Court held that a physically present co-occupant's stated refusal to permit entry renders a warrantless search unreasonable and invalid as to him, notwithstanding another occupant's consent.

In California v. Acevedo (1991) the Court held that police may search a container within an automobile without a warrant where they have probable cause to believe it holds contraband or evidence, with the search limited to the container and areas where the object could be.

In Missouri v. McNeely (2013) the Court held that the natural dissipation of alcohol in the bloodstream does not constitute an exigency in every drunk-driving case sufficient to justify a warrantless blood draw, and that exigency in this context must be determined case by case on the totality of the circumstances.

In Lange v. California (2021) the Court held that pursuit of a fleeing misdemeanor suspect does not always - that is, categorically - qualify as an exigent circumstance justifying a warrantless entry into a home.

In Camara v. Municipal Court (1967) the Court held that a municipal housing inspector needs a warrant to enter a dwelling over the occupant's objection, but that probable cause for such an area-inspection warrant may rest on reasonable legislative or administrative standards rather than on knowledge of conditions in the particular dwelling.

In South Dakota v. Opperman (1976) the Court held that the routine inventory of a lawfully impounded automobile, conducted following standard police procedures, is not unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment.

In Skinner v. Railway Labor Executives' Assn. (1989) the Court upheld Federal Railroad Administration regulations requiring blood and urine tests of covered employees after major train accidents, describing the government's interest in the conduct of employees engaged in safety-sensitive tasks as a special need beyond normal law enforcement that may justify departures from the usual warrant and probable-cause requirements.

In Rakas v. Illinois (1978) the Court held that Fourth Amendment rights are personal and may not be vicariously asserted, and folded the question formerly labeled standing into the substantive inquiry whether the person claiming the Amendment's protection had a legitimate expectation of privacy in the invaded place; the petitioners, who asserted no interest in the car or the items seized, could not challenge the search.

The phrase 'reasonable suspicion' appears in Terry v. Ohio only in Justice Douglas's dissenting opinion; the majority's operative language is 'specific and articulable facts' together with 'rational inferences from those facts'.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Fourth Amendment's warrant clause makes warrantless searches presumptively unlawful, or whether reasonableness is the sole touchstone.
positions: Katz stated that searches conducted outside the judicial process, without prior approval by judge or magistrate, are per se unreasonable subject only to a few specifically established and well-delineated exceptions - language Gant quoted approvingly in 2009.

The text itself contains no general warrant command; Carroll (1925) sustained a warrantless vehicle search on probable cause alone, and Kentucky v. King (2011) framed the Amendment as imposing two express requirements - that searches and seizures be reasonable, and that warrants issue only on probable cause with particularity.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both: the Court's stated presumption in favor of warrants alongside the textual point that the Amendment forbids unreasonable searching rather than warrantless searching, and treats the exception list as the practical content of that tension rather than as a footnote.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Katz privacy test replaced the older property-based understanding of a search.
positions: Katz declared the trespass doctrine of Olmstead and Goldman 'no longer controlling'.
Jones held that Katz added to, but did not substitute for, the common-law trespassory test, and decided the case on the property theory without reaching the privacy question.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as two live routes to the same threshold conclusion, which is how Jones itself frames the relationship. The lesson does not claim either test has been abandoned.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The status of the 'free to leave' language from United States v. Mendenhall.
positions: The formulation appears in Part II-A of Justice Stewart's opinion, joined only by Justice Rehnquist, and so commanded two votes in that case.
Later majority opinions, including Hodari D. and Bostick, treat the formulation as the governing test, with Bostick refining it for people who have no desire to leave.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the vote posture in Mendenhall and attributes the operative modern phrasing to Bostick, so students do not learn a plurality passage as a majority holding.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no legal content at all: it described 'Search, Seizure, And Warrants' as 'a foundational concept in Criminal Justice & Criminology' and defined it circularly as 'a foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson'. Nothing in it was verifiable because nothing in it was a claim about law.
The draft's vocabulary list (context, evidence, application) belonged to no legal framework and was discarded.
The draft's toolbox-drawer analogy and map-legend analogy carried no information about the Fourth Amendment and were discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with a Fourth Amendment framework built from the constitutional text and primary Supreme Court opinions read in full official PDFs.
Attributed the two-part reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test to Justice Harlan's concurrence in Katz rather than to the majority opinion, because the majority never states it in that form.
Recorded that the Mendenhall 'free to leave' passage drew only two votes in that case, and used Bostick's formulation as the operative modern statement.

Avoided the common textbook shorthand that Terry requires 'reasonable suspicion'; that phrase appears in Terry only in Justice Douglas's dissent, and the majority's operative language is 'specific and articulable facts'. The lesson notes that later cases supplied the label.
Stated Gant's rule in the Court's own two-branch form rather than as a flat prohibition on vehicle searches incident to arrest.
Noted that Riley preserves the exigent-circumstances exception, since the case is often taught as an absolute warrant requirement for phones.
Deferred the exclusionary rule's history, its other exceptions, and the deterrence debate to the published constitutional-protections lesson to avoid duplicating it.

Expanded the exception survey to the doctrines the topic assignment requires and the first draft omitted: Jardines on curtilage, Randolph on a present occupant's refusal, Acevedo on containers, McNeely and Lange on the refusal to treat exigency as categorical, Camara, Opperman and Skinner on searches with a purpose other than criminal investigation, and Rakas on standing.
Moved special-needs, administrative and standing doctrines out of the out-of-scope list, where the first pass had placed them, and into the lesson's core scope.

Supports: Roberts, C.J., for the Court, joined by Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan, JJ., with Alito, J., concurring in part and in the judgment; the consolidation with United States v. Wurie, No. 13-212; the holding that police generally may not, without a warrant, search digital information on a cell phone seized from an individual who has been arrested; the reasoning that digital data cannot itself be used as a weapon and that officers may examine a phone's physical aspects to ensure it is not a weapon; the closing instruction 'get a warrant'; and the Court's statement that the continued availability of the exigent circumstances exception may justify a warrantless search in particular cases.

sourceRecords.title: Carroll v. United States, 267 U.S. 132 (1925)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Reports
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Official bound-volume PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally. Supports: Taft, C.J., for the Court; the holding that the right to search a vehicle for illicit liquor does not depend on the right to arrest the offender in the first instance and that the seizure is legal if the officer stopping and searching the vehicle has reasonable or probable cause for believing it carries contraband; and the historical reasoning that contemporaneously with the adoption of the Fourth Amendment the first, second and fourth Congresses distinguished between goods concealed in a dwelling house and like goods in course of transportation in a movable vessel that could readily be put out of reach of a search warrant.

sourceRecords.title: Horton v. California, 496 U.S. 128 (1990)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Reports
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Official bound-volume PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally. Supports: Stevens, J., for the Court, joined by Rehnquist, C.J., and White, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia and Kennedy, JJ., with Brennan, J., dissenting joined by Marshall, J.; the holding that the Fourth Amendment does not prohibit the warrantless seizure of evidence in plain view even though its discovery was not inadvertent; and the restatement of the conditions that do apply - the essential predicate that the officer did not violate the Fourth Amendment in arriving at the place from which the object could be plainly viewed, plus the requirements that the object's incriminating character be immediately apparent and that the officer have a lawful right of access to the object itself.

sourceRecords.title: Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Reports
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Official bound-volume PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally. Supports: argued December 12, 1967, decided June 10, 1968; Warren, C.J., for the Court; the facts of Detective McFadden's observation of repeated window-casing and the subsequent pat-down; the holdings that whenever a police officer accosts an individual and restrains his freedom to walk away he has seized that person, and that a careful exploration of the outer surfaces of a person's clothing in an attempt to find weapons is a search; the requirement that in justifying the intrusion the officer 'must be able to point to specific and articulable facts which, taken together with rational inferences from those facts, reasonably warrant that intrusion'; the instruction to give weight not to an officer's 'inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or hunch' but to specific reasonable inferences; and the weapons-frisk standard of whether a reasonably prudent man in the circumstances would be warranted in believing his safety or that of others was in danger. A text search confirmed the phrase 'reasonable suspicion' appears in this opinion only in Justice Douglas's dissent, which is why the lesson attributes that label to later cases.

sourceRecords.title: Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643 (1961)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress, United States Reports volume 367 (official bound-volume scan)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record reused with its registered URL. Used in this lesson only for the single point that evidence obtained by a search or seizure violating the Federal Constitution is inadmissible in a state criminal trial, which is what makes the Fourth Amendment framework operative against state and local police. The rule's history and its other exceptions are taught in the constitutional-protections lesson.

sourceRecords.title: United States v. Leon, 468 U.S. 897 (1984)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress, United States Reports volume 468 (official bound-volume scan)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record reused with its registered URL. Used in this lesson only for the good-faith exception - that the exclusionary rule does not bar the prosecution's case-in-chief use of evidence obtained by officers acting in objectively reasonable reliance on a warrant issued by a detached and neutral magistrate but ultimately found invalid - and for the limits the Court preserved, including that the magistrate must not serve as a rubber stamp and that a knowingly or recklessly false affidavit remains open to challenge.

sourceRecords.title: Oregon v. Hass, 420 U.S. 714 (1975)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office (govinfo), United States Reports
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Official bound-volume PDF downloaded and text-extracted locally. Supports: Blackmun, J., for the Court, joined by Burger, C.J., and Stewart, White, Powell and Rehnquist, JJ.; and the Court's statement, citing Cooper v. California and Sibron v. New York, that 'a State is free as a matter of its own law to impose greater restrictions on police activity than those this Court holds to be necessary upon federal constitutional standards,' with the qualification that a State may not impose such greater restrictions as a matter of federal constitutional law. Cited only for the federal-floor point; the case's self-incrimination holding is outside this lesson's scope.

sourceRecords.title: Florida v. Jardines, 569 U.S. 1 (2013)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF and text-extracted locally. Supports the claim that taking a drug-detection dog onto a home's front porch is a search on the property/trespass route, that the porch is the classic exemplar of curtilage, and that curtilage is treated as part of the home. Verified: Scalia, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, joined by Thomas, Ginsburg, Sotomayor, and Kagan, JJ.

sourceRecords.title: Georgia v. Randolph, 547 U.S. 103 (2006)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF. Supports the limit on third-party consent: a physically present co-occupant's stated refusal to permit entry prevails, rendering the warrantless search unreasonable and invalid as to him. Verified: Souter, J., delivered the opinion of the Court.

sourceRecords.title: California v. Acevedo, 500 U.S. 565 (1991)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF. Supports the extension of the automobile exception to containers: police, in a search extending only to a container within an automobile, may search the container without a warrant where they have probable cause to believe it holds contraband or evidence. Verified: Blackmun, J., delivered the opinion of the Court.

sourceRecords.title: Missouri v. McNeely, 569 U.S. 141 (2013)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF. Supports the claim that exigency is not categorical: in drunk-driving investigations the natural dissipation of alcohol in the bloodstream does not constitute an exigency in every case sufficient to justify a warrantless blood draw, and exigency must be determined case by case on the totality of the circumstances. Verified: Sotomayor, J., delivered the opinion of the Court (Parts I, II-A, II-B, and IV for a majority).

sourceRecords.title: Lange v. California, 594 U.S. 295 (2021)
sourceRecords.provider: Supreme Court of the United States
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the supremecourt.gov opinion PDF (preliminary print paginated to 594 U.S. 295); govinfo has no downloadable bound volume this high as of the check date. Supports the claim that pursuit of a fleeing misdemeanor suspect does not always - that is, categorically - justify a warrantless entry into a home, and that a case-by-case assessment of exigency is required. Verified: Kagan, J., delivered the opinion of the Court; decided June 23, 2021.

sourceRecords.title: Camara v. Municipal Court of the City and County of San Francisco, 387 U.S. 523 (1967)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF. Supports the administrative-search claim: an occupant has a Fourth Amendment right to insist on a warrant before a municipal inspector enters a dwelling, and probable cause for such an area-inspection warrant may rest on reasonable legislative or administrative standards rather than on suspicion about a particular building. Verified: White, J., delivered the opinion of the Court.

sourceRecords.title: South Dakota v. Opperman, 428 U.S. 364 (1976)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF. Supports the inventory-search claim: the routine inventory of a lawfully impounded automobile, conducted following standard police procedures, is not unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment. Verified: Burger, C. J., delivered the opinion of the Court.

sourceRecords.title: Skinner v. Railway Labor Executives' Assn., 489 U.S. 602 (1989)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF. The regulations at issue require blood and urine tests of covered railroad employees following certain major train accidents or incidents, and separately authorize breath or urine testing after certain safety-rule violations. Supports the special-needs claim: the government's interest in regulating the conduct of employees engaged in safety-sensitive tasks presents special needs beyond normal law enforcement that may justify departures from the usual warrant and probable-cause requirements. Verified: Kennedy, J., delivered the opinion of the Court.

sourceRecords.title: Rakas v. Illinois, 439 U.S. 128 (1978)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Supreme Court (via GPO govinfo)
sourceRecords.license: U.S. government edict; not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read in the bound-volume PDF. Supports the standing claim: Fourth Amendment rights are personal, the standing inquiry is properly subsumed in the substantive question whether the person claiming the Amendment's protection had a legitimate expectation of privacy in the invaded place, and passengers who asserted no property or possessory interest in the car or the items seized could not challenge the search. Verified: Rehnquist, J., delivered the opinion of the Court.
